MAGA lawmaker who called out Trump faces federal recount fight: report
articles.description: A Florida Democrat went to federal court Friday to keep Miami-Dade’s elections chief off the recount in his race against Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, after the official said Salazar would win either way, NBC News reported. Miami-Dade Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia told the Miami Herald on election night that “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount,” and that it was “possible but not probable” there were enough remaining ballots to flip the results. Salazar led Democrat Eliott Rodriguez by 1,103 votes as of Thursday evening, a 0.44-point margin narrow enough to trigger an automatic recount. Rodriguez’s complaint also asks for confirmation of an alleged family tie. His campaign says Salazar’s recount attorney, Robert Fernandez, is Garcia’s son-in-law. Deputy elections supervisor Juan Mendieta told NBC News, “There is no conflict. She is not recusing herself.” Salazar, who is also named in the suit, called Rodriguez an “election denier” on X Thursday night and accused him of trying to turn the recount into a “political circus.” Her office did not respond to NBC News’ request for comment. The race tightened in a district that both Salazar and Donald Trump won comfortably in 2024. In September, Salazar filmed a campaign ad outside the White House telling the president that some of his immigration enforcement efforts had “gone too far.” Trump criticized her after the ad in a 13-post Truth Social tirade — but later endorsed her before Election Day.

articles.title: Bruised Trump plots 2028 'influence' play after midterm shellacking: report
articles.description: President Donald Trump has privately told his advisers of a plan “aimed at salvaging his clout” after Republicans’ historic midterm defeat this week, one that would help him “influence elections in 2028 and beyond,” Axios reported Friday. Democrats flipped at least seven GOP-held Senate seats and, according to network projections, are on track to hold more than 250 House seats, handing the party control of both chambers in January. Trump’s plan, Axios exclusively reported, will involve continued fundraising for his political operation, either through his super PAC MAGA Inc. or through other venues. The operation would give Trump “a way to pressure GOP lawmakers who consider breaking with him as the president enters his lame-duck era,” much as it had leading up to the midterms with the defeat of Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX). Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton ousted Cornyn in a May runoff — then lost Tuesday to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988. MAGA Inc. spent in excess of $400 million on the midterms, Axios reported, citing an unnamed source “familiar with the totals.” The super PAC had $164 million remaining in its coffers as of Oct. 14, though it's unclear how much was spent in the weeks leading up to the midterms and how much remains. Wealthy donors poured hundreds of millions into MAGA Inc. — many later benefited from administration decisions — but that money could dry up after Tuesday’s losses. “Raising money could become much harder with Democrats controlling Congress and major donors beginning to look [to turn] their attention toward 2028,” Axios’ report reads. “Republicans say Trump's diminished political clout will make it harder to attract the enormous checks that have flowed into MAGA Inc. The prospect of congressional investigations into alleged pay-for-play arrangements involving donors to Trump's political operation could further discourage contributions.”

articles.title: After the midterms, the global right is reeling. But the danger of Trumpism will never be gone | Jonathan Freedland
articles.description: Yes, the Republicans suffered humiliating defeat. But the fact that a Trump presidency was even possible means something like it could happen again He’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad. Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats in the popular vote for the House of Representatives was greater even than the 11.2% swing recorded in the Watergate midterms of November 1974, following the resignation in disgrace of Richard Nixon. Trump had worked hard for many months to undermine these elections, either by gerrymandering districts in his favour or preparing the ground for a later claim the vote was rigged, but to no avail: the democratic system proved too resilient, and the American public too determined to have their say. And have it they did, in a voice loud and clear. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
